extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and practitioners (particularly biotech/pharma applicants and EPO/PCT filers), IP attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on the formal requirements for patent drawings under the PCT and EPC, with emphasis on how those rules apply (or fail to apply) to scientific data, graphs and photographs used in biotechnology and pharmaceutical patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of patent drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of patent drawings is to aid understanding of an invention; embodiments of a mechanical invention may be easier to explain and understand as a drawing compared to a lengthy description. The European Patent Office (EPO) considers good quality drawings as very important for the correct disclosure of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings serve to communicate the invention to the skilled person. The article contrasts mechanical technical illustrations (where drawings naturally serve this purpose) with scientific data (which serve a different purpose and may not naturally conform to drawing requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presented to admit direct reproduction (Rule 11(a) PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings, like all other parts of the application, must be 'presented as to admit of direct reproduction by photography, electrostatic processes, photo offset, and microfilming, in any number of copies' (Rule 11(a) PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a functional/formal requirement aimed at ensuring reliable reproduction by standard reproduction processes. It underpins many of the subsequent specific formatting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution in durable black lines without colorings (Rule 11(a) PCT / Rule 46 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: '(a) Drawings shall be executed in durable, black, sufficiently dense and dark, uniformly thick and well-defined, lines and strokes without colorings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is well suited to mechanical technical illustrations but problematic for scientific figures (e.g., bar charts, shaded plots) where color or shading is used to distinguish elements. To comply applicants often must replace colors/shading with intrusive cross-hatching or otherwise alter the original data presentation, which can reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special drawing requirements enumerated (Rule 11.3 (a)-(n) PCT and Rule 46 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The special requirements relating to drawings are provided by Rule 11.3 (a)-(n) PCT and Rule 46 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page does not list every subrule but indicates these provisions are drafted with mechanical inventions in mind and contain specifics governing format, lines, scales, etc. Applicants should consult the full rules for detailed formal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow sheets and diagrams deemed to be drawings (Rule 46(3) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Flow sheets and diagrams shall be deemed to be drawings' (Rule 46 (3) EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This EPC provision helps to accommodate certain non-mechanical graphical representations (e.g., software flowcharts, process diagrams) by explicitly treating them as drawings under the rule set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs and scales generally disfavoured (Rule 11(f) PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11 (f) PCT states that a scale (even a graphical one) should only be drawn in 'exceptional' cases; graphs in general are not looked on favourably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should avoid including scales/graphs unless clearly exceptional; relying on graphs to show data may encounter formal objections and require conversion to a more acceptable format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour, shading and hatchings — differing PCT and EPO approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT: 'Color photographs are not accepted, nor are color drawings' (PCT applicant’s guide, 5.159). EPO Guidelines: 'the use of shading in figures is allowed provided this assists in their understanding and is not so extensive to impede legibility' (A-IX 7.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT is strict against colour; applicants often must replace shades/colour differences with cross-hatching or other black-and-white indicators. EPO is more permissive on shading but balance is needed: shading allowed only if it assists understanding and does not impede legibility. The practical difference can create uncertainty and extra work for applicants filing internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographs allowed only where drawings impossible; colour/photo handling differs
rubrics_metrics.description: PCT applicant’s guide: photographs are allowed 'where it is impossible to present in a drawing what is to be shown' and 'must be black and white...Color photographs are not accepted' (5.159). EPO Guidelines: photographs may be permitted 'where it is impossible to present in a drawing what is to be shown...Colour photographs are accepted, but will be scanned, printed and made available via file inspection only in black and white' (A IX 1.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where photographs are used include crystalline structures, western blots, immuno-fluorescence, or photos of modified organisms. Under PCT such photos must be B/W; EPO accepts colour initially but treats the official reproduction/inspection as B/W, which can impair the communicative value of colour data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical burden and risk of refusal for non‑conforming drawings (Rule 48 EPC / Article 90(5) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the EPO finds that the drawings provided do not satisfy Rule 46 EPC, they issue an invitation to remedy the deficiencies within 2 months (Rule 48 EPC). If the defect is not remedied on time or properly, the application will be refused (Article 90 (5) EPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may face significant time and expense to convert or reformat scientific data to meet formal drawing requirements; failure to comply can result in refusal of the application, so procedural deadlines and the cost of remediation are relevant practical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of scientific data for 'drawing' formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific data (e.g., bar charts, western blots, immuno‑fluorescence) are not suited for representation with black lines only and do not serve the same purpose as mechanical drawings; the phrase 'drawings' seems inappropriate for the types of graphical illustration provided in support of software, biotechnology and pharmaceutical inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that scientific data often cannot be meaningfully conveyed under current drawing formalities and suggests considering submission of such data under a different category (e.g., supplementary data analogous to scientific articles) so that the skilled person can read and understand the data without being forced into inferior black-and-white cross-hatched figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on whether a skilled person can read and understand the data (functional disclosure standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the purpose of data is to demonstrate the plausibility of a claimed effect, what matters is whether a skilled person would be able to read and understand the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a functional perspective suggesting that formal compliance should not override the substantive requirement of enabling and disclosing sufficient information. It is offered as an argument for rethinking rigid formal drawing rules for scientific data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency and discretionary application by receiving sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of a specific provision in the EPC means that the extent to which scientific data will be expected to conform to Rule 46 EPC requirements can be open to the whim of the EPO Receiving Section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be aware of possible inconsistent treatment, leading to unpredictable invitations to remedy; extra time and cost may be required to respond to discretionary objections.
